html:
The Ponca are a Native American nation of the Great Plains, today split between the Ponca Tribe of Nebraska and the Ponca Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma. They speak a Dhegiha Siouan language shared with the Omaha.

By their own history, the Ponca, Omaha, Kaw, Osage and Quapaw were one people living further east until the mid 1600s. Pushed by the Beaver Wars, they moved west across the Mississippi and split apart. By the late 1700s the Ponca had settled at the mouth of the Niobrara River, where it joins the Missouri, farming maize and hunting bison.

In 1877 the United States forced them from their land in Dakota Territory to Indian Territory. Hundreds died on the march and in the first years there; it is called the Ponca Trail of Tears. In 1879 the chief Standing Bear walked back to Nebraska to bury his son. Arrested, he sued, and a federal judge ruled that an Indian is a person under the law, a landmark case. His followers became the Ponca of Nebraska; most others stayed in Oklahoma under White Eagle.
